A 25-year-old woman comes to the hospital due to worsening dyspnea.  The patient was previously healthy; 2 months ago, she delivered a healthy baby boy at 38 weeks gestation.  Her arterial blood gas analysis shows evidence of hypoventilation.  During further evaluation, she is asked to take several maximally deep breaths, and the following physiologic information is obtained:

Which of the following locations is the most likely site of this patient's disease?​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌
explanation:
The above graph shows phrenic nerve signaling and the corresponding diaphragm response (ie, contraction to produce a more negative intrapleural pressure).  The patient's results show progressive attenuation of the intrapleural pressure (ie, progressively weaker diaphragmatic contractions) despite no decrease in nerve activity, which could potentially be caused by primary respiratory muscle fatigue (due to increased work of breathing from severe obstructive/restrictive lung disease) or impaired neuromuscular transmission; onset in the postpartum period is suggestive of myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disorder that impacts the neuromuscular junction.

In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors cause fatigable muscle weakness as acetylcholine stores within the presynaptic nerve terminal become progressively depleted with repetitive stimulation.  Although weakness in myasthenia gravis most commonly impacts the eyes (eg, diplopia), bulbar muscles, and/or extremities, it can manifest as respiratory failure (ie, myasthenic crisis), as seen in this patient.

(Choice A)  Impairment of the respiratory control centers in the brainstem can result in decreased frequency and/or amplitude of involuntary respirations (Ondine curse).  Voluntary breathing is unaffected.

(Choice B)  Nasopharyngeal lesions are unlikely to cause inspiratory airflow obstruction severe enough to cause rapid diaphragmatic fatigue because the oropharynx remains unobstructed (allowing the patient to breathe from the mouth).

(Choices D and E)  Metastatic disease to the pericardium could compress the phrenic nerve along its course.  In addition, the phrenic nerve can be affected by peripheral neuropathy.  However, both diseases cause uniform, weak inspirations during maximal voluntary ventilation rather than progressively weaker (ie, fatigable) diaphragmatic contractions.

Educational objective:Progressively weakening diaphragmatic contractions during maximal voluntary ventilation with intact phrenic nerve stimulation indicate neuromuscular junction pathology (eg, myasthenia gravis) or abnormally rapid primary muscle fatigue (eg, severe obstructive/restrictive lung disease).​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌
